extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, students and critics of drama and poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating poetic drama (especially tragedy), covering origins, definition, parts, unity, plot construction, measures, and the relation of poetry to history. Useful for playwrights, poets, and literary students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation as the origin and basis of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation is natural to man and is the cause which gave birth to poetry; all men delight in imitation because acquiring knowledge is pleasurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle argues that imitation (mimesis) is innate from childhood; people enjoy accurate resemblances (e.g., pictures of savage beasts). This grounds why poetry (an imitative art) pleases: it teaches/enquires about what things represent. Include examples or accurate resemblances to engage pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony and rhythm as natural causes of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Harmony and rhythm (with versification being part of rhythm) are natural to humans and contributed to the invention of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Versification arises from natural propensity for rhythm and harmony; those fitted by nature improved extempore effusions into poetry. Ensure rhythm/melody are present and suited to the poetic form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry originates from extempore songs and was gradually perfected
rubrics_metrics.description: Original poetry grew from extemporaneous effusions (rude songs at festivals) and was gradually improved by those naturally inclined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the historic emergence of forms (iambic for satire, hexameter for heroic) and how social/ceremonial contexts shaped forms. Use this to justify spontaneous or oral-feel elements if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genres arise from authors' temperaments and subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets of graver mind imitate honourable actions (serious/heroic subjects); looser-tempered poets treat the adventures of bad men and satirical iambics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match subject matter to poetial temperament and measure: serious actions to heroic/epic/tragedy, satirical attacks to iambic/comedic meter. Consider historical measures' affinities (iambic for invective/abuse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is the imitation of a noble and perfect action, of proper magnitude; expressed in agreeable language; produced by actors (not narrative); effecting a refinement of the passions of pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tragedy must focus on a complete, significant action, use language with rhythm/harmony/melody, be enacted rather than merely told, and aim to evoke/guide pity and fear (catharsis). Evaluate a play by whether it meets these elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six parts of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy has six parts from which it derives its quality: the story (plot), the manner (character), the discourse (diction), the sentiment (thought), the scenery (spectacle), and the melody (song).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these as explicit evaluation/ construction dimensions. Aristotle also frames instruments/modes: discourse and melody are the instruments of imitation; manner is the mode; subjects of imitation are story, scenery, and sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority/ranking of parts (plot first)
rubrics_metrics.description: The putting together of actions (the story/plot) is of the greatest importance; next comes manner (character), then sentiment (thought), discourse (diction), melody, and scenery (least important).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When revising or judging drama, prioritize plot coherence and the connection of actions above eloquent diction or scenic effects. Melody adds pleasure but spectacle depends little on the poet's art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy imitates actions, not men; actions determine happiness or misery
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is imitation of actions (human life, happiness and misery), because happiness consists in action; manners/character are secondary as causes of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design drama around consequential actions: the moral/psychological qualities matter only insofar as they produce actions that lead to consequences. Avoid treating a play as merely a collection of moral sayings or character sketches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia and recognition as essential dramatic devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Peripeteia (revolutions/changes of fortune) and recognition (acquired knowledge among characters) are parts of the story that attract attention and are important to tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include well-crafted reversals and recognitions to heighten emotional impact and to structure the plot toward catastrophe or resolution; these are harder to master than diction and often distinguish great tragedians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and 'a whole' (beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: A whole (a complete action) must have a beginning (not after anything else), a middle (following one thing and preceding another), and an end (which follows and is followed by nothing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct plots with clear causal sequence so that removing or changing any part alters the whole; ensure the story's parts are properly ordered and interdependent to preserve unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper magnitude/length (unity of time guideline)
rubrics_metrics.description: The action must be of proper magnitude — neither too short (not worth remembering) nor too long (memory/attention lost). Tragedy should as far as possible be comprehended within one revolution of the sun (roughly a day).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a temporal scope that the audience can perceive as a single coherent whole; scale the number of incidents to fit memorability and dramatic focus. Avoid sprawling plots that make the beginning forgettable before the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: A story should imitate a single entire action (unity of action)
rubrics_metrics.description: The story of a poem should be the imitation of a single, entire action; the parts ought to be so arranged that taking away any part would change or destroy the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid bundling many unrelated actions or the full life of a hero into one piece; select and arrange incidents so they all contribute causally to the central action. Episodes may be allowed but only if properly connected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry should treat what might have happened (probability/necessity), not merely facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet does not relate only what actually happened (as the historian does), but what might or could have happened according to probable or necessary consequence; poetry treats general principles, history particular facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inventing events, maintain plausibility (probability or necessity) rather than slavish adherence to historical fact; craft causes and motives to reveal general truths about human character and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid episodic stories (episodes without causal connection)
rubrics_metrics.description: An episodic story, where introduced episodes are neither probable nor necessary to each other, is the worst—common to bad poets and sometimes introduced by good ones to satisfy actors/contest requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prune episodes that do not advance the central action; resist adding incidents solely to lengthen the piece or to showcase actors. Each episode must serve the unity of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy is enacted by actors — performance elements belong when acted
rubrics_metrics.description: Since actors produce imitation, decorations (scenery), melody and discourse form parts of the tragedy in performance; some elements belong only when acted and not when read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish written poetic quality from performative effects: certain scenic or musical elements enhance performance but are not essential to the poetic art. When preparing a script, note which effects are intrinsic to the poem and which are stage-dependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discourse (diction) and melody defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Discourse (diction) is the arrangement of measures/words (an explanation of meaning by word-choice) and melody is that which makes effects manifest to all; both contribute to imitation but serve different pleasures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work on diction to clarify meaning (verse or prose) and on musical/melodic qualities to produce additional pleasure; however, diction ranks below plot/character in determining tragic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenery (spectacle) is attractive but least tied to poetic art
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenery (including dresses, machinery and stage effects) is very attractive to attention but depends little on the poet's art; the force of tragedy exists without performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on spectacular stage effects to compensate for poor plot or character; scenic artistry often lies with the scene-painter and technicians rather than the poet. Use spectacle to support, not substitute for, the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure selection: iambic best fitted for conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: When dialogue was introduced, nature suggested the iambic as the proper measure because the iambic is best adapted for conversation (we pronounce many iambics in ordinary speech).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose verse forms that fit the dramatic function: conversational scenes suit iambic rhythms, while heroic/narrative forms align with hexameters. Match meter to register and function in the drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of comedy and the ludicrous
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy is the imitation of men worse than ourselves in the ludicrous part of the vile; the ludicrous consists of some error and deformity which does not occasion pain or death (e.g., a hideous but uninjured face).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For comic writing, target faults that provoke laughter without cruelty or serious harm; distinguish comedic deformity/error from tragic suffering. Comedy's development and devices (masks, prologues) evolved separately from tragedy.
